data.title: Trump Says He'd Love to See Jensen Huang Back at Nvidia — WSJ
data.description:
By WSJ Staff

President Trump, taking questions from reporters at the White House Friday, said Nvidia's CEO search should include a very familiar name: Jensen Huang.

"I think there are very few people at that company that could do" what Huang, the former CEO, did, Trump said. "He put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."

Huang resigned earlier this month after a scandal involving extramarital affairs with with a suspected Chinese spy and an employee.

"We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them," Trump added. "I think the company if they were smart they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work."

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Union Pacific engineers' union wins nearly $100 million for schedule rule violation
data.description:
A union representing locomotive engineers at railroad operator Union Pacific has won a $98.8 million payout over a contract violation, the International Brotherhood of Teamsters said on Friday.

The Special Board of Adjustment, an arbitration tribunal, ruled that Union Pacific failed to implement a new work rule meant to ensure consistent scheduling, negotiated by its locomotive engineers' union in 2023, Teamsters said.

  • In 2023, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET) of the Teamsters Rail Conference negotiated an "11/4" schedule of 11 working days followed by 4 days off

  • The union said the company did not implement the policy within the mandated deadline, nor did it request an extension

  • The tribunal directed Union Pacific to pay each claimant one basic day's pay, based on their applicable assignment, for every calendar day they claimed during the period when the 11/4 benefit was denied

  • The period during which the benefit was denied ran from June 30, 2024, to January 27, 2025

  • Union Pacific is required to calculate the final payments owed within 30 days, Teamsters said

  • The company did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment

data.title: Wall Street banks set for banner year as Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs generate $1 billion in fees
data.description:
Key points:
  • Some banks learned of their fee the night before IPO, source says
  • Anthropic's fee deal shows issuers' power over Wall Street
  • Mega-deals pay a fraction of the up to 7% underwriting fee for smaller deals

By Sabrina Valle and Echo Wang

Wall Street banks are on track for one of their most lucrative years in the IPO business, with blockbuster listings by Anthropic and SpaceX generating more than $1 billion in underwriting fees alone.

A syndicate of 22 banks is set to collect about $550 million for underwriting Anthropic's $81.3 billion IPO, eclipsing the roughly $500 million they earned on SpaceX's record-setting offering in June, according to Anthropic's final offering prospectus published on Thursday.

The fees represent a relatively small share of the $81 billion Anthropic raised at its debut, or as much as $93.5 billion with overallotment options exercised. The banks will receive about 0.68% of the money raised in Anthropic's IPO, broadly in line with the roughly 0.67% they collected on SpaceX's offering.

Underwriting fees on IPOs typically run as high as 7% of proceeds, though the percentage drops sharply for bigger deals, with companies raising tens of billions of dollars able to negotiate significantly lower rates than smaller issuers.

ANTHROPIC'S FEE POOL

Anthropic's fee arrangements also highlight the bargaining power that blockbuster issuers hold over Wall Street.

Some banks working on the deal did not learn how much they would earn until Wednesday night, according to a person close to the transaction - suggesting an unusual degree of uncertainty until the final stages of the offering, even as banks compete fiercely over the most coveted deals.

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

While it is common for IPO fees to be finalized when an offering closes, it is unusual for a company not to communicate in advance an approximate percentage of the offering that underwriters can expect to receive, the person said.

Other high-profile issuers have kept banks in the dark until the final stages of an offering, using intense competition among underwriters for roles on prized deals.

SoftBank-owned chip designer Arm did not provide banks with a clear fee arrangement when it hired 28 underwriters for its $5 billion IPO in 2023, Reuters reported at the time. SoftBank waited until days before pricing to spell out the fee structure, giving it a better sense of how the banks had performed during the marketing process, according to a person familiar with the information.

Banks are willing to accept relatively low fees on mega-IPOs because of the prestige of working on landmark listings, the boost to their league-table rankings and the potential for additional business, including stock trading, lending and wealth management services.

Anthropic is paying $536.7 million of the underwriting fees, with the remaining $13.3 million paid by its seven co-founders, who sold shares in the offering, the prospectus showed.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which jointly led both the Anthropic and SpaceX IPOs, are set to take home the largest share of the fee pool, receiving roughly 20.5% each, or 41% combined, amounting to more than $110 million each. The remaining fees will be split among the other banks involved in preparing the AI company’s public debut.

MEGA-IPOS

Banks have already had a lucrative year from public offerings. Global IPOs raised more than $357 billion this year, according to Dealogic, up from $186 billion in 2025, with SpaceX and Anthropic alone accounting for about half of that.

That marks the second-biggest year for IPOs according to Dealogic data going back to 1995, behind 2021's haul of $609 billion.

Revenue from US IPOs for banks is also at its highest in five years, Dealogic data shows. Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan lead the rankings and have each earned more than $330 million so far this year excluding Anthropic's IPO, up from about $260 million apiece in 2025.

That is still far below 2021, when the three banks earned more than $1 billion in fees each and total US IPO revenue for US banks hit almost $10 billion, according to Dealogic.

The 2021 total was pushed up by a pandemic-era boom fuelled by near-zero interest rates, stimulus-driven retail trading and a wave of listings of blank-check companies.

data.title: Anthropic’s IPO debut not a success; won’t do well without infrastructure to support it – Dan Niles
data.description:
Tech investor Dan Niles is pushing back on the narrative that Anthropic's initial public offering was a success, arguing the AI company's stock performance and valuation raise red flags for investors.

The Niles Investment Management founder and portfolio manager told CNBC that he attempted to short Anthropic shares when the stock was up 30% on its first trading day but could not find shares available to borrow.

Niles pointed to the stock's trading pattern as cause for concern. While Anthropic finished its first day up 17%—above the 10 to 15% range typically considered a successful IPO—the shares opened up 34% before sliding throughout the session.

"The bad thing is for a successful IPO, you want to see it open and then continue to climb during the day," Niles said, adding that "the sellers were more aggressive at the open versus anybody who wanted to step into it."

The veteran investor questioned Anthropic's valuation of roughly 20x trailing revenues, contrasting it sharply with other AI-related investments.

"You can buy it at 20x trailing revenues or calendar 26 revenues, or you could go buy Samsung or Hynix at 2x trailing earnings," Niles said.

He argued that all these companies are connected to the same AI trade, noting, "You're not going to have Anthropic do great without the infrastructure to support it."

Niles also highlighted regulatory headwinds facing AI infrastructure expansion. He pointed to 40 out of 41 local initiatives that passed to slow down data center growth as a major obstacle.

"You can't have the growth that people are talking about when you have that going on," he said. "You have nowhere to put the actual chips."

Despite the stock nearing its $83 IPO price in its first full trading session, Niles remained skeptical about whether it would hold that level.

The broader market backdrop adds to his concerns, with the Nasdaq pacing for its worst week in over a year and turning negative year to date.

data.title: Trump Says He Will Penalize Companies That Build Data Centers Outside the U.S. — WSJ
data.description:
By Natalie Andrews and Philip Wegmann

WASHINGTON — President Trump said the federal government would penalize companies that build data centers in other countries, a move he said was meant to encourage the construction of the facilities in the U.S. to better compete with China on AI.

"We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday. "And we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it."

Trump said his administration would "fight very hard" to encourage companies to build data centers in the U.S., warning that those that build them in other countries would face "a tremendous tax."

Opposition to data centers became a hot-button issue in the midterm elections, with many voters saying they didn't want them built in their communities, worried the facilities would increase electricity bills.

Trump said communities should welcome the construction of data centers and negotiate deals to "make them pay you."

data.title: Binance hack laundering accelerates as $149M in Bitcoin passes through coinjoins, Elliptic says
data.description:
The people behind the Binance theft appear to have found the fast-forward button. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic says at least 2,310 BTC tied to the October 29 heist, worth approximately $149 million at the time, has now been pushed through coinjoin mixing transactions.

The more telling detail is the timing. Roughly 90% of that mixing activity took place in the week before Elliptic's November 20 update, which means the laundering operation just shifted from a slow simmer to a rolling boil.

A coinjoin works a bit like a group of strangers dumping identical bills into one bag and each pulling out the same amount. On a blockchain, many users combine their coins into a single transaction, making it much harder to trace which output belongs to which input.

According to Elliptic, the mixing here uses Wasabi Wallet-style techniques coordinated by Kruw. Wasabi is a privacy-focused Bitcoin wallet built around this kind of pooled transaction, and coordinators are the services that organize the rounds.

One wrinkle stands out. The Bitcoin being mixed is mostly not the Bitcoin that was originally stolen.

Instead, Elliptic says the mixed funds largely come from swaps of other stolen assets, including ETH, XRP and SOL. The attackers are converting a grab bag of tokens into Bitcoin first, then running that Bitcoin through the mixer.

The surge in mixing followed a large movement of Ether. Around 488,000 ETH, valued at approximately $860 million, was transferred out of five wallets linked to the theft.

Not long after, about $70 million of that was swapped into Bitcoin and sent into the mixing process. That sequence offers a fairly clear look at the pipeline: move the Ether, convert a slice to Bitcoin, then scramble it.

Even with the acceleration, most of the money has not gone anywhere near a cash register yet. Elliptic says it is tracking about $2.35 billion still sitting in addresses connected to the theft.

Meanwhile, an estimated $2.85 billion has been frozen or seized out of the overall $6.43 billion stolen. Elliptic's data also points to minimal cash-out activity so far.

According to the research, the pattern mirrors earlier incidents linked to the same actor, where stolen funds pass through several rounds of mixing and other privacy tools before anyone tries to cash out.

In those prior cases, the eventual exit tended to run through over-the-counter (OTC) channels, and it played out over long stretches of time. OTC desks handle large trades directly between parties rather than on a public order book, which can make big conversions less visible.

data.title: Global Payments jumps on report GTCR considering $50B takeover bid
data.description:
Global Payments (GPM) soared 14% after a report that GTCR is evaluating a takeover of the payments company.

GTCR is working with a group of other buyout firms to finance a possible transaction, according to a Bloomberg report on Friday, which cited people familiar with the matter. The deal would be worth about $50 billion, including debt and a premium.

A final decision hasn’t been made, according to the report. GTCR formerly worked with fellow PE firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice on a joint deal for Global Payments but has dropped that effort. GTCR is Global Payments' biggest holder with a 16% stake.

Representatives for GTCR and Global Payments didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from Bloomberg. CD&R declined to comment.

The latest update comes after Reuters reported last Thursday that CD&R and GTCR dropped their pursuit of the payments company. Late last month, the Financial Times reported that CD&R and GTCR were pursuing a take-private of the payments processor.

data.title: Christian Dior board approves Agache merger terms
data.description:
Christian Dior said on Friday its board had approved the terms of the planned merger of family holding company Agache into Christian Dior, as well as the company's conversion into a limited joint-stock partnership.

The move advances the ownership simplification plan unveiled by the Arnault family in September.

Shareholders will vote on the transaction on December 30, while the merged listed entity would directly hold 49.76% of LVMH's share capital and 65.55% of voting rights.

Christian Dior also confirmed that the Arnault family group would launch a cash tender offer for the shares it does not already own, without a squeeze-out, if the conversion is completed.

The offer price will be based on 95% of Christian Dior's net asset value and determined on December 23, with a filing expected in January 2027 and a potential launch in the first quarter of 2027.

data.title: Canada Hands Ford $300 Million After Finishing Plant Retooling
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada on Friday unveiled over $300 million in financing to Ford Motor after the automaker began production of its F-Series Super Duty pickup truck at a Toronto-area factory that underwent retooling prior to President Trump's hefty automobile tariffs.

Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly said the money underscores the government's efforts to maintain an auto sector in the country in the face of hefty tariffs from President Trump. The plant in Oakville, Ontario, was closed starting in 2024 for retooling to allow for the manufacturing of conventional and electrified versions of the Super Duty truck.

Ford's decision to follow through with production is in contrast to Stellantis, which is now engaged in a row with Joly and other Canadian officials. Stellantis received federal funding for a retooling of two of its Canadian factories. Stellantis then pivoted and shifted planned production of the Jeep Compass in Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois amid Trump's trade policy. Stellantis has struck a deal to sell the factory in Brampton, Ontario, to a local defense firm.

Ford's Oakville decision "was an act of resistance. Canadians know a lot about resistence these days," said Joly, in reference to the automaker's push to build pickup trucks in Canada amid a trade row with Washington.

"Our strategy is based on our clear conviction that Canada is an auto nation and intends to continue to do so," Joly said at a formal reopening of the Oakville plant. "We will continue to invest in automakers that invest in us."

Stellantis has offered to repay some of the money Canada provided for past support. Stellantis Chief Executive Antonio Filosa is set to speak with Joly later Friday, and the Canadian minister reiterated her threat to launch a lawsuit against the automaker unless it reconsiders its plans for Brampton. "If they go ahead and sell the plant, well, then they will face legal recourses from the government of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars," she told reporters in Oakville.

She added Canada is open to provide Stellantis with additional financial support should it choose to maintain operations in Brampton.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com

data.title: Expert’s AI prompts in environmental lawsuit must be disclosed, US judge rules
data.description:
By Mike Scarcella

A US federal judge on Friday ruled that an expert witness for an environmental group suing a Shell Oil subsidiary in a climate-related lawsuit must turn over details about her use of AI in ​the case.

Here are the details:

  • The ruling by US District Judge Vernon Oliver in Connecticut affirms a federal magistrate’s decision that said the expert, Naomi Oreskes, must turn over prompts used to produce a witness report for plaintiff Conservation Law Foundation

  • Oliver said the AI prompts that Oreskes or her team used to sort through large numbers of documents comprise “the basis” for her opinions. The judge said the prompts are distinguishable from notes related to draft material that might otherwise be shielded from disclosure

  • The decision is part of a growing number of disputes over whether and when an expert witness must disclose AI prompts

  • Opposing parties in ​litigation often try to undermine each other’s experts. Requiring disclosure of AI-assisted research could open new avenues to argue that an expert’s analysis ​is flawed or unreliable

  • Conservation Law ⁠Foundation and Oreskes did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Shell also did not immediately respond to a request for comment

  • Shell has denied wrongdoing in the lawsuit, which alleges that its terminal in New Haven, Connecticut, risks exposing nearby neighborhoods and waterways to hazardous chemicals during flooding

The case is Conservation Law Foundation Inc v Shell Oil Products US et al, U.S. ⁠District Court ​for the District of Connecticut, No. 3:21-cv-00933-VDO.

data.title: Sky Protocol sees $2 billion in stablecoin withdrawals, disputes illicit fund claims
data.description:
Sky Protocol processed more than $2 billion in stablecoin redemptions on Thursday, the same day a CoinDesk investigation linked $518 million in transactions through the protocol to illicit activity.

The withdrawals involved users exchanging Sky’s USDS stablecoin for Circle’s USDC through its Peg Stability Module (PSM), a system that allows users to swap the tokens at a fixed rate.

Sky, which has a total value locked (TVL) of $2.3 billion, said on Friday in a statement that USDS maintained its $1 peg throughout the withdrawals. According to the protocol, the amount of USDC held in the PSM never fell below $800 million and had climbed back above $1.1 billion by Friday.

Sky also challenged the investigation, pointing to a review by Block Analitica, which notably serves as a risk adviser to the Sky ecosystem.

The withdrawals came amid concerns raised by the investigation that Circle could freeze USDC held by Sky, potentially making it harder for users to redeem their stablecoins.

Related: Circle freezes $12.6M of USDC linked to privacy protocol Zama

Sky disputes findings on illicit transactions

CoinDesk’s Nov. 19 report looked at research by blockchain analytics firm Inca Digital, which identified $518 million in transactions involving wallets linked to hackers, sanctioned entities, and other threat actors over a span of five years.

Of that amount, around $101.9 million was linked to North Korean actors, including wallets connected to the February 2025 Bybit hack.

Meanwhile, Block Analitica disputed some parts of the investigation, saying that the $518 million represented less than 0.06% of the more than $960 billion processed through Sky’s peg stability modules.

The firm said about two-thirds of the flagged activity occurred between 2021 and mid-2024 – before Sky introduced its newer LitePSM system.

Block Analitica also questioned the reported links to North Korean threat actors, stating that some wallets were several transactions removed from known addresses and may have belonged to unrelated users.

The firm added that most of the flagged transactions passed through trading services such as 1inch, ParaSwap and MetaMask Swaps, which automatically choose where to route trades.

Sky says reserves remain strong despite withdrawals

The large withdrawals also came amid a sharp drop in the number of USDS tokens in circulation. The supply fell nearly 40% in one day to about 3.2 billion tokens, according to DefiLlama data. However, the stablecoin maintained its $1 value despite the decline.

CoinDesk reported that a wallet linked to crypto exchange Poloniex accounted for a large share of the withdrawals, although it wasn’t clear whether the exchange itself was behind the transactions.

The combined circulating supply of Sky’s USDS and DAI stablecoins fell to $6.11 billion as of Nov. 20, down 37.8% over the past 30 days. Source: Sky Ecosystem Financial Insights

Sky said it held about $9.3 billion in assets backing its stablecoins as of Friday, compared with around $6.11 billion in USDS and DAI in circulation, according to its financial dashboard. The dashboard also showed about $93 million in reserves to help cover potential losses.

Cointelegraph reached out to the Sky Frontier Foundation for comment but had not received a response by publication.

data.title: European emissions proposal faces Middle East pushback at UN aviation agency
data.description:
By Allison Lampert

Plans to change the European Union's Emissions Trading System faced pushback at a global aviation gathering that wraps up on Friday, as Middle East countries challenged fresh efforts to curb pollution from airlines outside an existing deal.

It is the latest revolt within the aviation sector over plans to expand Europe's biggest climate change policy to cover flights to third-country destinations within 5,000 km (3,107 miles) of Frankfurt Airport, starting in 2029. The ETS currently applies to flights within the European Economic Area.

Saudi Arabia urged International Civil Aviation Organization member countries to support a global approach to countering emissions under the decade-old Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. Saudi Arabia wants CORSIA, an ICAO program that is mandatory for most airlines, to be the only emissions plan covering international aviation.

Qatar also proposed that ICAO undertake a technical assessment of the implications of the EU ETS for CORSIA.

Several European countries disagreed with the two Middle East countries' positions.

Under CORSIA, airlines in most countries have to buy offsets in environmental projects to counter their rising emissions from international flights.

The airline industry has pledged to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, but executives acknowledge the target will be difficult to hit due to shortages of green jet fuel and increasing passenger traffic.

Airlines and most countries support CORSIA to avoid a patchwork of emissions programs that they argue would raise costs. But some European lawmakers and environmental groups have argued CORSIA does not go far enough to reduce international aviation emissions.

Under the EU proposal, the 5,000-km distance would cover flights to airports in the Middle East and North Africa but omit transatlantic flights to the United States.

Saudi Arabia, supported by Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt, urged countries and regional organizations to avoid overlapping and double charging under "duplicative or extraterritorial emissions trade schemes that will increase compliance costs, create administrative burdens and distort competition."

ICAO cannot impose rules on its 193 member states, but its decisions influence national regulations.

data.title: China's BYD has SUV that infringes on JLR Defender design, Dutch court rules
data.description:
By Nick Carey

A judge at the Dutch district court in The Hague ruled on Friday that a large SUV made by BYD infringes on the design of Jaguar Land Rover's popular Defender model and imposed a temporary injunction prohibiting the Chinese automaker from selling the vehicle in the European Union.

JLR, a unit of India's Tata Motors , launched the case earlier this year after BYD announced on its UK web site that the seven-seater Ti7 SUV was available for orders with deliveries to customers starting in January 2027.

BYD launched the Fangchengbao Ti7 in China last year.

"In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover," the court ruling said. "The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7."

The temporary injunction is for a week because the court found that BYD "currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU."

The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD's affiliate in the United Kingdom.

It is rare in Europe for major automakers to go to court over design rights infringement. It is also uncommon for such a ruling to come so early in proceedings of a case that is ongoing and likely to last for some time.

"We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary," JLR said in a statement. "Legal proceedings are ongoing, and we won’t be commenting further at this time."

Legacy automakers have often complained that Chinese automakers have copied designs, though little has been proven in court. In 2005, for instance, General Motors and Chinese rival Chery settled a case over the Chery QQ that the No. 1 US automaker said was a copy of its Chevrolet Spark.

In a statement, BYD said it "strongly disagrees" with the ruling and will appeal it.

"The BYD Ti 7 is the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights," BYD said. "We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect."

BYD has grown rapidly in Europe since launching sales on the continent in late 2022. According to ACEA data, this year through September the Chinese automaker's sales more than doubled to over 280,000 vehicles in Europe versus the same period last year, outselling Ford, Tesla and Nissan.
